What was wrong with java.util.Date and Calendar?

They are mutable, so not thread-safe, and shared instances can change. Months are 0-based and years in the deprecated constructor are offset by 1900. Date is really an instant with a misleading toString. Invalid values roll over silently. There are no separate types for date-only, time-only or duration values. SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe.
Why is SimpleDateFormat not thread-safe? How do you fix it in legacy code?

It stores intermediate state in an instance Calendar field during format and parse, so threads overwrite each other, giving wrong dates or exceptions. Reproduced on Java 21: 8 threads sharing one instance gave bad results. Fixes: move to DateTimeFormatter (best), create one per call, use a ThreadLocal, or synchronize.
LocalDateTime vs ZonedDateTime vs OffsetDateTime vs Instant?

LocalDateTime is a wall clock reading with no zone, so it does not name a moment. OffsetDateTime adds a fixed offset and so names a moment. ZonedDateTime adds zone rules, and can do DST-correct arithmetic. Instant is a point on the UTC timeline, with no human fields. Log and store events as Instant; use ZonedDateTime for calculations in a location; use OffsetDateTime in API payloads.
Is LocalDateTime appropriate for an event timestamp?

No. Without a zone, "2024-11-03T01:30" in New York is two different moments, and two servers in different zones produce incomparable values. Use Instant. LocalDateTime fits scheduled local times, along with a stored zone ID.
Predict the output. LocalDate j = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 31); System.out.println(j.plusMonths(1)); System.out.println(j.plusMonths(1).plusMonths(1)); System.out.println(j.plusMonths(2));

2024-02-29
2024-03-29
2024-03-31
The day is clamped to the month's end. The second line starts from Feb 29, so it stays at 29. Date arithmetic with months is not associative.
Predict the output. var a = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15); var b = LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 20); System.out.println(Period.between(a, b).getDays()); System.out.println(ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(a, b));
5, then 65. Period is P2M5D, and getDays returns only the days component. ChronoUnit.DAYS gives the total. Mixing them up is a very common bug.
Predict the result. LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1); d.plusDays(1); System.out.println(d);
2024-01-01. The object is immutable; the result of plusDays was thrown away.
What is the difference between Duration and Period? When does it matter?

Duration is exact seconds and nanos, and Period is calendar units. Across DST, plus(Period.ofDays(1)) keeps the same wall clock, whereas plus(Duration.ofDays(1)) adds exactly 24 hours. Noon before the US spring change gave 12:00 and 13:00 respectively on the next day. A subscription uses Period; a cache TTL uses Duration.
What does Duration.between(LocalDate, LocalDate) do?
It throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException: Unsupported unit: Seconds, as dates have no time component. Use Period.between or ChronoUnit.DAYS.between, or convert with atStartOfDay().
Why can you not do Instant.now().plus(1, ChronoUnit.MONTHS)?

The length of a month depends on the calendar and zone, and Instant has neither. It throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException: Unsupported unit: Months. Convert first: instant.atZone(zone).plusMonths(1).toInstant().
What happens with 02:30 on a day when the clocks skip from 02:00 to 03:00? And when an hour repeats?

For the gap, ZonedDateTime.of moves the time forward by the gap's length: 03:30-04:00 in New York on 2024-03-10. For the overlap, it keeps the earlier offset by default (summer time), and withLaterOffsetAtOverlap() selects the other. Adding one hour to the first 01:30 yields the second 01:30. If a schedule must not skip or duplicate, check getValidOffsets.
Offset vs time zone?

An offset (+02:00) is a number at one moment. A time zone (Europe/Paris) is a set of rules mapping any instant to an offset, including DST and historic changes. You can compute an offset from a zone and an instant, but not a zone from an offset, because many zones share one offset.
How should dates be stored in a database across time zones?

Past events: UTC timestamp, displayed in the user's zone. Set the JDBC and Hibernate time zone to UTC (hibernate.jdbc.time_zone), so JVM defaults do not alter data. Date-only: DATE with LocalDate. Future local appointments: local date-time plus an IANA zone ID, converting at display time, since zone rules can change. Never store abbreviations such as EST.
What does this print, and why is it a bug? LocalDate.of(2024, 12, 30).format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("YYYY-MM-dd", Locale.US));

2025-12-30. YYYY is the week-based year, and Dec 30 2024 falls in week 1 of 2025. It usually looks right in testing, and breaks only around New Year. Use uuuu or yyyy. The same goes for mm (minutes) and DD (day of year).
Does this parse? LocalDate.parse("2023-02-30"); LocalDate.parse("2023-02-30", DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("uuuu-MM-dd"));

The first throws DateTimeParseException: … Invalid date 'FEBRUARY 30', because the built-in ISO formatter is STRICT. The second returns 2023-02-28: ofPattern uses SMART, which clamps days 29 to 31 in shorter months. Add .withResolverStyle(ResolverStyle.STRICT) to reject it.
Why is DateTimeFormatter safe to share?
It is immutable, and parse state is created per call. A private static final instance is the normal approach. Methods such as withLocale return new instances.
equals vs isEqual for ZonedDateTime?

equals compares local date-time, offset and zone. isEqual compares the instant. 12:00Z and 17:30+05:30 are the same moment: equals is false, and isEqual is true. compareTo is also not purely instant-based: it returned -1 for these, after comparing the instant then the local fields.
What does LocalDate.of(2024,1,1).compareTo(LocalDate.of(2024,3,1)) return?
-2. It returns the difference of the first differing field, here months. Do not compare it to -1; only the sign is meaningful. Prefer isBefore or isAfter.
How do you make code using now() testable?

Inject a Clock (or InstantSource, Java 17) and call LocalDate.now(clock). Production wires Clock.systemUTC(), and tests use Clock.fixed(…). Mockito's static mocking of LocalDate.now works too, but is a worse design.
How would you calculate someone's age, or the last Friday of a month?

int age = Period.between(birthDate, LocalDate.now(clock)).getYears();
LocalDate lastFriday = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastInMonth(DayOfWeek.FRIDAY));
What is an annotation? What makes it "do" something?

Metadata with no behaviour. Effects come from a reader: the compiler (@Override), a processor at build time (Lombok, MapStruct), or runtime reflection (Spring's @Autowired). Technically, it is an interface extending java.lang.annotation.Annotation, and at runtime instances are dynamic proxies.
What are the retention policies? What is the default?
SOURCE: dropped by the compiler. CLASS: in the class file, not visible at runtime; this is the default. RUNTIME: readable by reflection. A framework annotation must be RUNTIME.
My custom annotation returns null from getAnnotation. Why?

Check, in order:
- Missing @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME).
- It sits on a method of a class, but you are inspecting a proxy or subclass. Spring's CGLIB proxies do not carry method annotations; use AopUtils.getTargetClass or AnnotationUtils.
- It is repeated, so the JVM wrapped it in the container. Use getAnnotationsByType.
- It is on a superclass, without @Inherited, or on an interface.
What can an annotation element's type be? Can a default be null?

Primitives, String, Class, an enum, another annotation, or a one-dimensional array of those. Defaults must be constants, and cannot be null. Elements cannot have parameters or throws. Annotations cannot extend others or be generic.
Predict what these return. @Role("a") @Role("b") class Two {} Two.class.getAnnotation(Role.class); Two.class.getAnnotationsByType(Role.class).length;
null and 2. Repeated annotations get wrapped in the container @Roles. getAnnotationsByType looks through the container, and also finds a single use.
Does @Inherited work on interfaces or methods?
No. It works only for annotations on classes, with subclasses via extends. Tested: a class implementing an annotated interface had 0 annotations, and an overriding method had 0.
Annotation processors vs runtime reflection?

Processors run in javac, can generate source files and report compile errors, and add no runtime cost, so startup is faster and they suit native images. They work only with what is known at compile time. Reflection works on anything at runtime, but with a startup cost, errors appearing late, and native-image friction. This is why Micronaut and Spring AOT shift to compile-time generation.
How does Lombok work if processors cannot change classes?

The official API only creates new files. Lombok uses a processor as an entry point, then casts to javac's internal classes and modifies the abstract syntax tree before code generation. It is effectively a compiler hack, so it depends on JDK internals. Since records arrived, many of its uses have gone. With recent JDKs, make sure Lombok is explicitly set as an annotation processor.
getMethods vs getDeclaredMethods?

getMethods: all public methods, inherited included. getDeclaredMethods: all methods declared in this class, of any visibility, with no inherited ones. Order is unspecified. To scan the full hierarchy, loop over getSuperclass(). Bridge and synthetic methods also appear, so filter with isBridge and isSynthetic.
Class.forName vs ClassLoader.loadClass vs .class?

Class.forName(name) loads and initializes (runs static blocks). loadClass and the .class literal load it but do not initialize. Test output confirmed this. Class.forName(name, false, loader) lets you choose. Reading a constant such as static final int K = 5 does not initialize the class either, since the value is inlined.

Can reflection change a private final field? Predict x(). class Fin { private final int x = 1; int x() { return x; } } var f = Fin.class.getDeclaredField("x"); f.setAccessible(true); var o = new Fin(); f.set(o, 2); System.out.println(o.x()); System.out.println(f.get(o));

Prints 1, then 2. The set worked, but 1 is a compile-time constant, so the compiler inlined it in x(). For a final field set in a constructor, x() shows 2, though JIT trust of final fields can make this unreliable. static final and record fields refuse this, with IllegalAccessException. Newer JDK work aims to restrict changing finals further, so do not depend on it.
What is InvocationTargetException?

A checked wrapper thrown by Method.invoke and Constructor.newInstance when the called code itself throws. It separates "reflection failed" from "the target failed". getMessage() is null, as verified, so logging only the message hides everything. Use getCause().
Why do you get InaccessibleObjectException after upgrading Java?

Since Java 16 and definitely Java 17, JDK internals are strongly encapsulated. A library calling setAccessible on java.base internals fails. Upgrade the library first, and if needed add a narrow --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED, tracked as technical debt.
Can reflection break a singleton? Which singleton resists it?

Yes: setAccessible on a private constructor makes another instance, for a class in your own code. Add a guard in the constructor which throws if the instance exists. An enum singleton is safe: the reflection API refuses to construct enums, and serialization preserves identity.
How does reflection affect performance, and how do frameworks handle that?

A reflective call is typically tens of times slower than a direct one in a tight loop, because of boxing, arrays, and reduced inlining, but that is nanoseconds. The bigger cost is scanning and metadata reading at startup. Frameworks cache Method objects, generate bytecode (Hibernate's ByteBuddy-based accessors) or use build-time generation. Never optimize this without profiling.
Write a dynamic proxy that measures method duration.
JDK proxy vs CGLIB? Why can't a final class be proxied by Spring?

JDK proxies implement interfaces. CGLIB generates a subclass and overrides methods. A final class cannot be subclassed, and final methods cannot be overridden: those calls run on the proxy instance with uninitialized state, and without advice. Spring Boot defaults to class-based proxies. Kotlin classes, final by default, need the kotlin-spring plugin.
Why does this.method() skip @Transactional?

The annotation is applied by a proxy outside your object. Internal calls use this, the raw target, so no interceptor runs. Move the method to a separate bean; or inject self lazily; or use TransactionTemplate. The same applies to @Async and @Cacheable.
What is a MethodHandle? How is it different from reflection?

A strongly typed, invocable reference to a member. Access is checked at lookup, and a static final handle inlines like a direct call. It has no discovery ability, so frameworks often use reflection to find a member, then unreflect it to a handle to invoke it quickly. Exceptions pass straight through.
Why does Object r = add.invokeExact(1, 2); fail with WrongMethodTypeException?

invokeExact is signature polymorphic: the compiler records the call's types from the source, including the return type. Here the call site is (int,int)Object, while the handle is (int,int)int. Write int r = (int) add.invokeExact(1, 2); or use invoke.
How does ServiceLoader work? Where is it used?

It reads META-INF/services/<interface> files on the class path, and provides clauses for modules, then lazily instantiates each provider, which must be public with a public no-arg constructor (or a provider() method for modules). Used by JDBC 4 drivers, SLF4J 2, and annotation processors. It allows a plug-in design: adding a JAR adds a feature, with no code change in the consumer.
Why does "TITLE".toLowerCase() sometimes not equal "title"?

It uses the default locale. In Turkish, I lowercases to dotless ı. So use toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) for keys, protocol values and enum names. Verified with Locale.forLanguageTag("tr"). For case-insensitive comparison, use equalsIgnoreCase.
How does ResourceBundle pick a file? What are the main i18n pitfalls?

It tries the requested locale from most to least specific, then the default locale the same way, then the base bundle. Pitfalls: a server default locale leaking into output; concatenating translated fragments, instead of using full messages with placeholders; a single quote in MessageFormat; plurals needing rules; dates and numbers formatted with a default locale; and assuming that text length is stable in a UI.
Design question: how would you implement a simple dependency injection container?

- Scan classes for @Component, using a classpath scanner, or ServiceLoader, or a compile-time index.
- Build a definition for each: its class, the constructor annotated @Inject (or the single constructor), and dependencies from getParameterTypes.
- Instantiate in dependency order: computeIfAbsent in a singleton map, keeping an "in creation" set to detect cycles.
- Inject fields annotated @Inject with setAccessible(true), though constructor injection avoids this.
- Wrap beans with a Proxy if methods have advice annotations.
- Resolve generics using getGenericParameterTypes, so that Repository<User> selects the right bean.
Discuss trade-offs: startup time from scanning, and the alternative of compile-time generation.
Scenario: scheduled jobs run an hour off after a DST change, and some ran twice. How do you fix it?

Likely causes: the job uses a fixed offset or stores a next run time in UTC computed by adding 24 hours, or the job's cron runs in local time inside the skipped or repeated hour. Fixes: state the zone explicitly (Spring's @Scheduled(cron = "…", zone = "Europe/Amsterdam")); avoid scheduling between 01:00 and 03:00 local time; or run in UTC if the business does not depend on local time. Compute "same time tomorrow" with ZonedDateTime.plusDays. For the duplicates, make jobs idempotent with a run key for the logical date.
Scenario: a startup got slow as the codebase grew, and a profiler shows annotation scanning. What can you do?

Limit component scan paths, and avoid scanning all JARs. Use a compile-time index or Spring AOT processing. Consider class data sharing (AppCDS). Make rarely used beans lazy. Reduce classpath size. For serverless, consider a GraalVM native image, keeping in mind that reflection hints are then required. Measure with Spring Boot's startup actuator endpoint (BufferingApplicationStartup), not by guessing.
How do you measure elapsed time in Java? Why not System.currentTimeMillis() or Instant.now()?
Your Angular client sends "2025-03-01T00:00:00.000Z" for a date of birth, and the server stores 28 Feb. What went wrong?

The client serialised a local midnight as an instant (JavaScript Date.toISOString() converts to UTC), so a user east of UTC sends the previous day, and the server converts it again. A date of birth is a calendar date with no zone: send "2025-03-01" and bind it to LocalDate. Reserve Instant/OffsetDateTime for moments in time.
Jackson throws "Java 8 date/time type java.time.LocalDate not supported by default". Why, when Spring Boot works?

A plain new ObjectMapper() does not register JavaTimeModule (jackson-datatype-jsr310). Spring Boot's auto-configured mapper does, so the error usually means code created its own mapper. Inject the Spring-managed ObjectMapper, or call registerModule(new JavaTimeModule()) (or findAndRegisterModules()) and disable WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS.
Where do annotations on a record component end up?

An annotation on a record component is propagated to every element it is applicable to, based on its @Target: the private field, the accessor method, the canonical constructor parameter, and the record component itself (ElementType.RECORD_COMPONENT). That is why @NotNull or @JsonProperty on a record component work for validation and Jackson. Read them with getRecordComponents() and component.getAnnotation(…).
A JWT has "exp": 1735689600. How do you check whether it is expired?

JWT times are epoch seconds. Instant exp = Instant.ofEpochSecond(1735689600); then exp.isBefore(clock.instant().minus(skew)) with a small clock-skew allowance (for example 30–60 seconds). Inject a Clock so tests can control "now". Using ofEpochMilli here would put the expiry in January 1970 and reject every token.
MySQL DATETIME vs TIMESTAMP: which column for which java.time type?

| DATETIME | TIMESTAMP
What is stored | The wall-clock value exactly as given | A UTC point in time
Time zone conversion | None | Converted from the session time zone to UTC on write, and back on read
Range | Year 1000 to 9999 | 1970 to 2038-01-19 (UTC)
Natural Java type | LocalDateTime | Instant / OffsetDateTime
Fractional seconds | Up to 6 digits with DATETIME(6) | Up to 6 digits with TIMESTAMP(6)
Rule of thumb: for "when did this happen" store a UTC instant, and keep the JVM and the JDBC connection time zone fixed (usually UTC) so nothing shifts on the way. Use DATETIME, or DATE, for values with no zone, such as a date of birth or a clinic opening time, and mind TIMESTAMP's 2038 limit.
Marker interface vs annotation: how do you choose?

| Marker interface (e.g. Serializable) | Annotation (e.g. @Entity)
Defines a type | Yes: methods can accept only marked objects, checked by the compiler | No
Applies to | Classes and interfaces only | Classes, methods, fields, parameters and more
Carries data | No | Yes, elements like @Table(name = "x")
Inherited by subclasses | Always | Only class annotations marked @Inherited
Runtime check | instanceof, fast | isAnnotationPresent, needs RUNTIME retention
Rule of thumb: use a marker interface when you want the compiler to enforce "only these objects may be passed here". Use an annotation for everything else, especially framework metadata on methods and fields.
ServiceLoader vs Spring component scanning vs Class.forName: how does each find implementations?

| ServiceLoader | Spring scanning | Class.forName
How classes are found | META-INF/services/<interface name> file, or provides in module-info | Scans packages for @Component and friends | You supply the class name, e.g. from config
How they are created | Public no-arg constructor, or a static provider() method in modules | Constructor injection with dependencies | You call getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()
Dependencies needed | JDK only | Spring container | JDK only
Laziness | Lazy; stream() lets you inspect types before creating | Eager singletons by default | When you call it
Real users | JDBC drivers, SLF4J 2 providers | Your application beans | Old JDBC code, plugin loaders
Rule of thumb: ServiceLoader for a plain library that must find plug-ins without a framework, scanning inside a Spring app, and Class.forName only when the class name really comes from configuration.
